title: Kimble/Röwekamp, Legal Culture in European History 1860–1960

slides.title: The thesis: a law steeped in the male view — and yet a tool for women
slides.text: The introduction by Sara L. KIMBLE and Marion RÖWEKAMP to the volume NEW PERSPECTIVES ON EUROPEAN WOMEN'S LEGAL HISTORY. The opening thesis is, in the words of the legal theorist CATHARINE MacKINNON, that LAW ITSELF IS STEEPED IN MALE BIAS AND SHAPED BY MALE DOMINANCE — the laws were MADE BY MEN, INTERPRETED BY MEN AND UNTIL RECENTLY ENFORCED EXCLUSIVELY BY MEN. Together with religion and other patriarchal forces, law thus reinforced systems of power to the disadvantage of women. BUT — AND THE WHOLE BOOK RESTS ON THAT SECOND HALF OF THE THESIS — WOMEN AND MEN ALIKE USED LEGAL SYSTEMS, LEGAL KNOWLEDGE AND POLITICAL STRUCTURES TO VOICE RESISTANCE AGAINST THE INEQUALITIES LAW HAD CREATED OR ENTRENCHED. The authors therefore examine HOW LAW HELPS TO SHAPE THE SOCIAL CONSTRUCTION OF GENDER. The book has THREE PARTS: I. gender and power in FAMILY LAW in the century 1860–1960; II. THE ENTRY OF WOMEN INTO THE LEGAL PROFESSION in comparative perspective; III. INTERNATIONAL REFORMS bearing on the legal position of women.

cards.q: What is the twofold thesis of Kimble and Röwekamp's introduction?
cards.a: 1) Law is STEEPED IN MALE BIAS (MacKinnon) — the laws were made, interpreted and enforced by men, and together with religion reinforced patriarchal power. 2) AT THE SAME TIME women USED THE LAW THEMSELVES — legal knowledge and political structures served them to resist the inequalities law had created.
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

cards.q: How is the book divided?
cards.a: Three parts: I. gender and power in FAMILY LAW 1860–1960; II. THE ENTRY OF WOMEN INTO THE LEGAL PROFESSION in comparative perspective and its relation to the women's rights movement; III. INTERNATIONAL REFORMS prompted by or affecting the legal position of women.
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

slides.title: The paradox of codification: equality on paper, subordination in the statute
slides.text: The central research question of the whole book: HOW EUROPEANS RESPONDED TO THE NEW RESTRICTIONS ON WOMEN'S RIGHTS CREATED BY THE CODIFICATIONS OF THE LATE 18TH AND EARLY 19TH CENTURIES. And here is the point to memorise: THE UNEQUAL LEGAL POSITION OF WOMEN WAS ENTRENCHED IN FAMILY LAW PRECISELY AT THE MOMENT WHEN THE INTERESTS OF THE STATE BEGAN TO COMPETE WITH THOSE OF THE ESTABLISHED RELIGIONS. The family itself became A POLITICAL SITE, as liberal rights became linked to MASCULINITY in a way that worsened women's opportunities further. Three Enlightenment codifications proclaimed equality of the sexes: the CODEX MAXIMILIANEUS BAVARICUS OF 1756 says that 'human beings are divided by nature in various ways, above all into the male and the female sex… in general neither sex has precedence over the other'; the PRUSSIAN ALLGEMEINES LANDRECHT OF 1794, that 'the rights of both sexes are equal unless special laws or valid declarations of will provide exceptions'; and the AUSTRIAN ABGB OF 1811 does NOT MENTION equality of the sexes AT ALL, because its author FRANZ VON ZEILLER took it for granted that men and women are equal in private law. But those natural-law declarations of equality DID NOT PREVAIL OVER CUSTOM, where women remained subordinate to men in the family and in society.

cards.q: At what moment, on Kimble and Röwekamp's account, was the unequal position of women in family law entrenched?
cards.a: PRECISELY AT THE MOMENT WHEN THE INTERESTS OF THE STATE BEGAN TO COMPETE WITH THOSE OF THE ESTABLISHED RELIGIONS — that is, at the codifications of the late 18th and early 19th centuries. The family became a political site and liberal rights became linked to masculinity in a way that worsened women's opportunities further.
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

cards.q: How did the three Enlightenment codifications treat equality of the sexes?
cards.a: Codex Maximilianeus Bavaricus (1756): 'in general neither sex has precedence over the other'. The Prussian ALR (1794): 'the rights of both sexes are equal unless special laws provide exceptions'. The Austrian ABGB (1811) does NOT MENTION equality at all — Franz von Zeiller took it for granted. All three declarations, however, DID NOT PREVAIL OVER CUSTOM.
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

slides.title: The Prussian ALR 1794: progress immediately taken back
slides.text: Of the three, the PRUSSIAN ALR is regarded as PROGRESS for the legal position of women, because it ENDED THE EARLIER GESCHLECHTSVORMUNDSCHAFT — THE SEX GUARDIANSHIP (CURA SEXUS) OF MEN OVER WOMEN (§ 24, I 1). BUT the guardianship (CURA MARITALIS) WAS REINTRODUCED FOR MARRIED WOMEN IN SUBSEQUENTLY CODIFIED NORMS. Men were designated the LEGAL HEADS OF HOUSEHOLDS (§ 184 II, 1) and the code regulated the husband's authority over his wife down to intimate detail: the wife MANAGED THE HOUSEHOLD (§ 194, II, 1) and for work outside the home she NEEDED HER HUSBAND'S PERMISSION (§ 195 II, 1); both spouses were obliged to 'PERFORM THE MARITAL DUTY' (§ 178, II, 1) FOR THE PURPOSE OF PROCREATION (§ 1, II, 1) — the enforceability of that norm was doubtful, but it speaks to the social view of the reproductive mandate of marriage in a patriarchal society. The husband obtained CONTROL OVER THE MARRIED WOMAN'S PROPERTY (§ 205, II, 1), though she could secure by marriage contract a RESERVED ESTATE (VORBEHALTSGUT, §§ 206–209 and 221–230, II, 1). Some things were on the contrary better than before: DIVORCE WAS POSSIBLE IN CERTAIN CIRCUMSTANCES (§§ 668ff, II, 1), INCLUDING DIVORCE BY MUTUAL CONSENT (§ 716, II, 1), and the position of the UNMARRIED MOTHER AND HER CHILDREN was comparatively liberal. And an essential coda: THE GERMAN BGB OF 1900 TIGHTENED THE PRUSSIAN ALR AGAIN TO WOMEN'S DISADVANTAGE.

terms.def: The sex guardianship of men over women; the Prussian ALR abolished it (§ 24, I 1).
Marital guardianship over a married woman — reintroduced into Prussian law by later norms.
The reserved estate a married woman could secure for herself by marriage contract.

cards.q: In what was the Prussian ALR (1794) progress, and how was that progress taken back?
cards.a: It ended the GESCHLECHTSVORMUNDSCHAFT — the sex guardianship (cura sexus) of men over women (§ 24, I 1). BUT the guardianship CURA MARITALIS was REINTRODUCED FOR MARRIED WOMEN by subsequently codified norms, and the German BGB of 1900 TIGHTENED Prussian law further to women's disadvantage.
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

cards.q: How did the Prussian ALR regulate the position of a married woman in the household?
cards.a: The husband was the LEGAL HEAD OF THE HOUSEHOLD (§ 184 II, 1), the wife managed the household (§ 194) and for work outside the home NEEDED HIS PERMISSION (§ 195); both were obliged to 'perform the marital duty' (§ 178) for PROCREATION (§ 1); the husband obtained control over her property (§ 205), though she could reserve a VORBEHALTSGUT by contract (§§ 206–209, 221–230).
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

cards.q: What in the Prussian ALR was on the contrary better for women than before?
cards.a: DIVORCE WAS POSSIBLE IN CERTAIN CIRCUMSTANCES (§§ 668ff, II, 1), including DIVORCE BY MUTUAL CONSENT (§ 716, II, 1). The legal position of the UNMARRIED MOTHER AND HER CHILDREN was also comparatively liberal.
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

slides.title: The French took from the Prussians only the worse part
slides.text: French jurists were impressed by the Prussian ALR and used it as a model for their codes — BUT THEY DID NOT TAKE OVER THE LEGAL INSTITUTIONS FAVOURABLE TO WOMEN. At the same time they turned their backs on some revolutionary reforms concerning children. DURING THE REVOLUTION, after sharp legislative debates: IN 1791 WOMEN WERE FORBIDDEN TO BRING PATERNITY CLAIMS AGAINST A SEDUCER; IN 1793 A FATHER WAS PERMITTED TO RECOGNISE HIS ILLEGITIMATE CHILD, but IN 1794 on condition that such a child MAY NOT CLAIM AN INHERITANCE AT THE EXPENSE OF 'LEGITIMATE' CHILDREN. The revolutionaries also SECULARISED MARRIAGE AND LIBERALISED DIVORCE IN 1792. One of the drafters of the Code civil, JEAN-JACQUES RÉGIS DE CAMBACÉRÈS, designed it to reflect natural law and to establish liberty — BUT IN PRACTICE THE LAWS PRESCRIBED IDEALS AND REFLECTED CULTURAL AND SOCIAL NORMS. Napoleon likened women to property, indeed to fruit trees, 'destined to make children'.

cards.q: What did French jurists take from the Prussian ALR and what did they not?
cards.a: They were IMPRESSED by it and used it as a model — BUT THEY DID NOT TAKE OVER THE INSTITUTIONS FAVOURABLE TO WOMEN. At the same time they turned their backs on the revolutionary reforms concerning children.
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

cards.q: What did the revolution do with paternity, illegitimate children and marriage?
cards.a: 1791 it FORBADE women to sue a seducer for paternity; 1793 it allowed a father to RECOGNISE an illegitimate child; 1794 on condition that such a child MAY NOT CLAIM AN INHERITANCE AT THE EXPENSE OF 'LEGITIMATE' CHILDREN; 1792 it SECULARISED MARRIAGE AND LIBERALISED DIVORCE.
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

slides.title: The Code civil 1804 and the Penal Code 1810
slides.text: THE FRENCH CIVIL CODE (1804) AND PENAL CODE (1810) unified CANON, ROMAN AND CUSTOMARY LAW under Enlightenment principles and Napoleon's own patriarchal attitudes. URSULA VOGEL makes a sharp observation here: the drafters of the code legitimised THE INCAPACITY (INCAPACITÉ) OF WIVES AND STRENGTHENED MALE AUTHORITY (PUISSANCE MARITALE) BY USING A MODERN LANGUAGE THAT NATURALISED THE COMPLEMENTARITY OF THE SEXES AND SENTIMENTALISED MARRIAGE IN SUCH A WAY THAT INDIVIDUAL PROPERTY RIGHTS AND THE LEGAL EQUALITY OF MARRIED WOMEN COULD APPEAR PECULIARLY OUT OF PLACE. The marriage contract acquired a 'SECULAR SACREDNESS' which stripped it of its 'individualist and voluntarist elements' while strengthening the husband's control over his wife's person and property. In marriage the wife owed her husband 'OBEDIENCE' and he was charged with her 'PROTECTION' (ART. 213). The penal code imposed HARSH SANCTIONS ON WOMEN FOR ADULTERY, including imprisonment and divorce, so as to secure paternity for the transmission of property within the family. THE HUSBAND, BY CONTRAST, WAS EXCUSED IF HE MURDERED HIS WIFE AND HER LOVER WHEN HE CAUGHT THEM IN THE MARITAL HOME (ART. 324); his own extramarital relations were not restricted, unless he brought a mistress home. The code preserved from the revolution the CIVIL MARRIAGE as an affirmation of state authority — religious ceremonies were henceforth without legal effect. And divorce: REINTRODUCED ONLY IN 1884, limited to THREE GROUNDS — THE HUSBAND'S CONVICTION OF A CRIME, CRUELTY AND ADULTERY.

terms.def: The incapacity of the wife and marital power — the pair of institutions on which the position of the married woman in the Code civil rests.

cards.q: How, on Ursula Vogel's account, did the drafters of the Code civil legitimise the subordination of wives?
cards.a: BY A MODERN LANGUAGE THAT NATURALISED THE COMPLEMENTARITY OF THE SEXES AND SENTIMENTALISED MARRIAGE — thereby making INCAPACITÉ and PUISSANCE MARITALE look natural and individual property rights and the equality of married women look OUT OF PLACE. The marriage contract acquired a 'secular sacredness' and lost its individualist and voluntarist elements.
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

cards.q: What did art. 213 and art. 324 of the French codes provide?
cards.a: Art. 213 of the Code civil: the wife owes her husband 'OBEDIENCE', he is charged with her 'PROTECTION'. Art. 324 of the Penal Code (1810): THE HUSBAND WAS EXCUSED IF HE MURDERED HIS WIFE AND HER LOVER WHEN HE CAUGHT THEM IN THE MARITAL HOME — his own infidelity was not restricted unless he brought a mistress home.
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

cards.q: When was divorce reintroduced in France and on what grounds?
cards.a: IN 1884, limited to THREE GROUNDS: the husband's conviction of a crime, CRUELTY and ADULTERY. (The revolution had liberalised it in 1792, the Code civil then removed it; the code did, however, keep civil marriage from the revolution.)
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

slides.title: Napoleonic diffusion and Marianne Weber
slides.text: Through the Napoleonic wars (1803–1815) the influence of the French code spread to ITALY, THE NETHERLANDS, LUXEMBOURG, BELGIUM, SPAIN, PORTUGAL, ROMANIA, POLAND, PARTS OF GERMANY AND GREECE, and further to THE FRENCH COLONIES, QUEBEC, LOUISIANA AND MUCH OF LATIN AMERICA. Critics condemned the code for its inequalities — among them the German sociologist of law MARIANNE WEBER (1870–1954), for whom the code 'PRESERVED THE FEATURES OF MEDIEVAL PATRIARCHY IN THEIR LONGEST AND PUREST FORM'. (A useful detail from the notes: THE ITALIAN CODE DIFFERED FROM THE FRENCH IN NOT REGULATING DIVORCE — a decision protecting the state's relations with the Vatican, the CONCORDAT, and Vatican opposition delayed divorce reform UNTIL 1970.)

cards.q: How did Marianne Weber assess the Code civil?
cards.a: That it 'PRESERVED THE FEATURES OF MEDIEVAL PATRIARCHY IN THEIR LONGEST AND PUREST FORM'. Weber (1870–1954) was a German sociologist of law and among the code's sharpest critics.
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

cards.q: Why did the Italian civil code not regulate divorce, and how long did that last?
cards.a: To PROTECT THE STATE'S RELATIONS WITH THE VATICAN (the concordat). Vatican opposition delayed divorce reform UNTIL 1970.
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

slides.title: Coverture: a wife with no legal existence
slides.text: In the English common law the power relations of marriage were determined by the system of COVERTURE. The jurist WILLIAM BLACKSTONE put it famously: 'BY MARRIAGE, THE HUSBAND AND WIFE ARE ONE PERSON IN LAW; THAT IS, THE VERY BEING OR LEGAL EXISTENCE OF THE WOMAN IS SUSPENDED DURING THE MARRIAGE.' FROM THE EARLY 17TH CENTURY married women in England were DEPRIVED OF THE RIGHT TO MAKE CONTRACTS, since they were held to have no separate legal identity and no right to own property — UNLIKE THE UNMARRIED WOMAN, THE 'FEME SOLE'. UTE GERHARD adds an argument useful in an exam: THE LEGAL POSITION OF WIVES NOT ONLY CONTRADICTED THAT OF UNMARRIED WOMEN BUT WAS A FLAGRANT DEFIANCE OF ENGLAND'S EARLY CONSTITUTIONAL INSTITUTIONS — ITS PARLIAMENTARY TRADITIONS, THE SEPARATION OF POWERS AND THE CONSTITUTIONAL GUARANTEE OF PROPERTY — and with growing industrialisation and commercialisation it came under increasing pressure.

terms.def: The English institution under which a woman's legal existence is suspended by marriage and merged with her husband's.
An unmarried woman — unlike a wife she could own property and make contracts.

cards.q: Quote Blackstone on coverture and say what followed from it.
cards.a: 'By marriage, the husband and wife are ONE PERSON IN LAW; that is, the very being or legal existence of the woman is SUSPENDED during the marriage.' From the early 17th century married women in England were deprived of THE RIGHT TO MAKE CONTRACTS and of the right to own property — unlike the unmarried 'FEME SOLE'.
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

cards.q: What constitutional argument against coverture does Ute Gerhard formulate?
cards.a: That the position of wives not only CONTRADICTED THAT OF UNMARRIED WOMEN but was A FLAGRANT DEFIANCE OF ENGLAND'S EARLY CONSTITUTIONAL INSTITUTIONS — its PARLIAMENTARY TRADITIONS, the SEPARATION OF POWERS and the CONSTITUTIONAL GUARANTEE OF PROPERTY — and with industrialisation it came under increasing pressure.
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

slides.title: What exactly the criticism attacked
slides.text: Criticism of women's subordinate place in the national codes focused on THE INEQUALITIES OF MARRIAGE, especially on the denial to women of CONTROL OVER THEMSELVES AND THEIR CHILDREN, OVER THEIR EARNED INCOME AND OVER INHERITED PROPERTY. Crucially, THE LEGAL DISTINCTION BETWEEN THE MARRIED AND THE UNMARRIED WOMAN HAD FUNDAMENTAL CONSEQUENCES FOR THE ENJOYMENT OF THEIR RIGHTS — the inequality therefore ran not along the axis 'man/woman' but along the axis of MARITAL STATUS. Gender paradigms influenced the formalisation of family law in such a way that its provisions obstructed the recognition of women as INDIVIDUALS AND LEGAL PERSONS. The volume thereby shows THE COMMON LEGAL BACKGROUND OF THE EUROPEAN WOMEN'S RIGHTS MOVEMENT, even though the precise timing of the challenges differed in each context.

cards.q: What did the criticism of women's position in the European codes focus on?
cards.a: On THE INEQUALITIES OF MARRIAGE: the denial of control OVER THEMSELVES AND THEIR CHILDREN, OVER EARNED INCOME and OVER INHERITED PROPERTY. Fundamental consequences followed from THE LEGAL DISTINCTION BETWEEN THE MARRIED AND THE UNMARRIED WOMAN — the inequality ran not merely along the axis of sex but along that of marital status.
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

slides.title: The first wave of protest: from the Gazette des Femmes to Chauvin
slides.text: Protests against the subordination of married women under the Code civil began AS EARLY AS THE 1830s, when the GAZETTE DES FEMMES petitioned the king and the deputies for the reform of art. 213, arguing that under the CHARTER OF 1830 Frenchmen and Frenchwomen are 'EQUAL BEFORE THE LAW'. The campaign against the subjection of women was led by advocates connected with the SAINT-SIMONIANS. In Italy ANNA MARIA MOZZONI (1837–1920) criticised the NEW ITALIAN CIVIL CODE OF 1865 as harmful to women's rights; she recognised the power of law to 'place the fate of families in the hands of men' and at the same time its 'IMPOTENCE' to give men the capacity to lead a family. She also called for an end to state-regulated prostitution, TRANSLATED MILL'S 'THE SUBJECTION OF WOMEN' (1869) INTO ITALIAN (1879) and founded a cross-class association for women's rights (1881). In Poland ELIZA ORZESZKOWA (1841–1910) published the novel MARTA (1872) about a young widow trying to survive in a society that denies women basic rights, and then became a leading figure of the movement; in a later phase PAULINA KUCZALSKA-REINSCHMIT (1859–1921) urged divided reformers to make the reform of the civil code a priority. IN 1878 LÉON RICHER (1824–1911) and MARIA DERAISMES (1828–1894) broadened the critique of the legal oppression of women at the FIRST INTERNATIONAL CONGRESS ON WOMEN'S RIGHTS IN PARIS. At a conference IN 1889 the Belgian feminist MARIE POPELIN condemned the Code civil for 'degrading' women and consigning them to a sphere 'OUTSIDE THINKING HUMANITY'. And by 1896 the French feminist JEANNE CHAUVIN (1862–1926) could insist that LEGAL KNOWLEDGE IS INDISPENSABLE TO THE EMPOWERMENT OF WOMEN.

cards.q: What was the Gazette des Femmes' argument in the 1830s?
cards.a: It petitioned the king and the deputies for the reform of ART. 213 of the Code civil on the ground that under the CHARTER OF 1830 French men and women are 'EQUAL BEFORE THE LAW'. It is the earliest documented protest against the subordination of married women under the code.
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

cards.q: What did Anna Maria Mozzoni achieve?
cards.a: She criticised the NEW ITALIAN CIVIL CODE OF 1865, called for an end to STATE-REGULATED PROSTITUTION, TRANSLATED MILL'S 'THE SUBJECTION OF WOMEN' (1869) INTO ITALIAN (1879) and in 1881 founded a CROSS-CLASS ASSOCIATION for women's rights.
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

cards.q: How did Marie Popelin's condemnation of 1889 run?
cards.a: That the Code civil 'DEGRADED' women and consigned them to a sphere 'OUTSIDE THINKING HUMANITY'. Popelin was a Belgian feminist and herself a lawyer — she sought admission to the profession in vain all her life.
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

slides.title: 1904: the centenary and the burning code
slides.text: FOR THE CENTENARY OF THE PROMULGATION OF THE CODE CIVIL IN 1904 a coalition of feminists — HUBERTINE AUCLERT (1848–1914), CAROLINE KAUFFMANN (1840–1926), ELISKA VINCENT (1841–1914) and JEANNE ODDO-DEFLOU (b. 1856) — staged a series of disruptive protests. THEY ATTEMPTED TO BURN A COPY OF THE CODE ON THE PLACE VENDÔME IN PARIS and condemned its treatment of married women, who in rights are equal to 'MINORS, CONVICTS AND LUNATICS'. The code, they argued, therefore violates DEMOCRATIC PRINCIPLES, because it 'ENCOURAGES' men to 'destroy, oppress, diminish and exploit' women. Oddo-Deflou then carried her critique to an international audience in BELGIUM, from where those ideas spread further.

cards.q: What happened on the Place Vendôme in 1904 and why?
cards.a: A coalition of feminists (Auclert, Kauffmann, Vincent, Oddo-Deflou) attempted, FOR THE CENTENARY OF THE CODE CIVIL, TO BURN A COPY OF THE CODE. The argument: married women are in rights equal to 'MINORS, CONVICTS AND LUNATICS', and the code thereby violates democratic principles because it 'encourages' men to destroy, oppress and exploit women.
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

slides.title: Frauenlandsturm: the movement's most significant reform effort
slides.text: The German women's struggle against the civil code, the so-called FRAUENLANDSTURM, became THE MOST SIGNIFICANT REFORM EFFORT OF THE WHOLE MOVEMENT. Women attacked the BGB with a series of petitions. The BUND DEUTSCHER FRAUENVEREINE submitted a petition against the codification IN 1899, arguing: 'IN OTHER AREAS OF LAW WOMEN ARE RESPONSIBLE LEGAL PERSONALITIES; ONLY IN THE CASE OF MARRIAGE ARE THEY STILL UNDER THE GUARDIANSHIP OF MEN.' And further, in an argument worth knowing verbatim: WHEN SERFDOM AND FEUDALISM ENDED IN EUROPE, THE ONLY LEGAL SITUATION STILL ENSLAVING HUMAN BEINGS WAS THE MARRIAGE CONTRACT — IT GIVES THE HUSBAND IN ONE PERSON THE FUNCTIONS OF LEGISLATOR, JUDGE AND PARTY AND TAKES THE WIFE'S LEGAL PERSONALITY AWAY. Poor women in troubled or violent marriages faced acute danger. According to the German feminist ALICE SALOMON (1872–1948), marriage was tyranny for working-class women: 'SHE LIVES LIKE A PRISONER OR LIKE AN OLD DOG', and her only hope is 'THAT SHE WILL NOT BE BEATEN AND THAT HER HUSBAND WILL NOT DECEIVE HER'. Similar protests took place in AUSTRIA AND SWITZERLAND.

terms.def: The German women's struggle against the civil code (BGB) — the most significant reform effort of the women's movement.

cards.q: What was the key argument of the Bund Deutscher Frauenvereine's petition of 1899?
cards.a: That when SERFDOM AND FEUDALISM ended in Europe, the only legal situation STILL ENSLAVING HUMAN BEINGS WAS THE MARRIAGE CONTRACT — it gives the husband IN ONE PERSON the functions of LEGISLATOR, JUDGE AND PARTY and takes away the wife's legal personality. In other areas of law women are responsible legal personalities.
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

cards.q: What is the Frauenlandsturm?
cards.a: The German women's struggle against the civil code (BGB), conducted through a series of petitions — on the authors' account THE MOST SIGNIFICANT REFORM EFFORT of the whole women's movement. Similar protests took place in Austria and Switzerland.
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

slides.title: England: Caroline Norton and four statutes
slides.text: CAROLINE NORTON (1808–1877) defended herself against her husband's abuse and secured parliamentary statutes in women's favour: the CUSTODY OF INFANTS ACT (1839), the MATRIMONIAL CAUSES ACT (1857) and the FIRST MARRIED WOMEN'S PROPERTY ACT (1870). THE SECOND MARRIED WOMEN'S PROPERTY ACT (1882) largely ABOLISHED THE LAW THAT PLACED WIVES UNDER THEIR HUSBANDS' AUTHORITY: married women no longer had to surrender their personal property on marriage and could OWN, BUY AND SEPARATE IT — THEIR LEGAL IDENTITY AS INDIVIDUALS WAS RESTORED. BUT NOTE THE LIMIT OF THAT REFORM, for it shows just how far equality reached at the time: THE ACT DID NOT TOUCH THE PERSONAL RELATIONS OF SPOUSES — a wife was still 'bound to follow her husband's domicile at home and abroad and to live with him if he so required', and FATHERS CONTINUED TO ENJOY GUARDIANSHIP RIGHTS OVER THEIR CHILDREN; on divorce the court awarded guardianship to THE INNOCENT PARTY. The authors draw a general conclusion: IN THESE EXAMPLES WE SEE WOMEN'S LEGAL ACTIVISM AS THE CATALYST OF EVENTUAL REFORM.

cards.q: Which four English statutes are associated with Caroline Norton, and what did the last one do?
cards.a: The Custody of Infants Act (1839), the Matrimonial Causes Act (1857), the first Married Women's Property Act (1870) and the SECOND MARRIED WOMEN'S PROPERTY ACT (1882) — which largely ABOLISHED THE SUBORDINATION OF WIVES: women kept their personal property, could own, buy and separate it, and THEIR LEGAL IDENTITY WAS RESTORED.
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

cards.q: What did the Married Women's Property Act of 1882 NOT touch?
cards.a: THE PERSONAL RELATIONS OF SPOUSES: a wife was still bound to FOLLOW HER HUSBAND'S DOMICILE at home and abroad and to live with him if he required it, and FATHERS CONTINUED TO ENJOY GUARDIANSHIP RIGHTS over the children (on divorce the court awarded guardianship to the innocent party).
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

slides.title: Eastern and south-eastern Europe: inherited foreign laws
slides.text: The history of reform in eastern and south-eastern Europe is more complex. As GREECE, POLAND, CZECHOSLOVAKIA AND HUNGARY emerged or re-emerged from the constraints of multi-ethnic empires, THE NEW NATION STATES INHERITED 'FOREIGN' LEGAL SYSTEMS and had to cope with MULTI-ETHNIC, MULTICULTURAL AND MULTILINGUAL POPULATIONS LIVING UNDER DIFFERENT LEGAL TRADITIONS. At the same time internal struggles were under way, as ethnic minorities sought representation of their collective and separate identities within the state. And here is the idea you can take as the key to the whole of Part I: IN SEEKING TO RECONCILE THE VARIOUS MINORITIES, THE LEGISLATORS WRITING NATIONAL CIVIL CODES TRIED TO CLARIFY THE CONCEPT OF THE NATION — AND THEREFORE INSCRIBED INTO THEM THEIR NOTIONS OF THE PROPER GENDER ORDER. In GREECE (Doxiadis, ch. 1) legislators sought to follow the principles of the western European codes, which provoked a debate on the nature of the family to the detriment of women's rights — national codification there led to A DECLINE IN WOMEN'S PARTICIPATION IN COURT PROCEEDINGS.

cards.q: Why were the codifications in eastern Europe particularly difficult for women?
cards.a: The new states INHERITED 'FOREIGN' LEGAL SYSTEMS and multi-ethnic populations living under different legal traditions. IN SEEKING TO RECONCILE THOSE MINORITIES THE LEGISLATORS TRIED TO CLARIFY THE CONCEPT OF THE NATION — AND THEREBY INSCRIBED INTO THE CODES THEIR NOTIONS OF THE PROPER GENDER ORDER.
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

cards.q: What did national codification do in Greece?
cards.a: Legislators wanted to follow the western European codes, which provoked a debate on the nature of the family TO THE DETRIMENT OF WOMEN'S RIGHTS — and the codification led to A DECLINE IN WOMEN'S PARTICIPATION IN COURT PROCEEDINGS.
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

slides.title: Spain: reform against the will of the majority — and its reversal
slides.text: In Spain (Nielfa, ch. 2) a revolutionary government introduced reforms of women's rights AGAINST THE WILL OF THE MAJORITY. Historically Spanish society and law maintained conservative gender roles, above all through the influential role of the CATHOLIC CHURCH. WITH THE ESTABLISHMENT OF THE SECOND REPUBLIC IN 1931 parliament granted women THE VOTE and, with comparatively little opposition, passed laws equalising power relations in family law. THOSE REFORMS PROVED UNPOPULAR, HOWEVER, AND WERE REVERSED AFTER FRANCO'S COUP IN 1936. Spain restored equal rights for women in family law ONLY LATE IN THE 20TH CENTURY, after a renewed women's rights movement. (For the timeline: in the republican zone of the civil war THE FIRST WOMAN JUDGE was appointed in 1936.)

cards.q: What became of the Spanish family law reforms of 1931?
cards.a: The Second Republic granted women THE VOTE and equalised family law with little opposition — but the reforms were UNPOPULAR and were REVERSED AFTER FRANCO'S COUP IN 1936. Spain restored equal rights only late in the 20th century.
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

slides.title: Czechoslovakia: two chapters, one failure
slides.text: The state of CZECHOSLOVAKIA, created IN 1918 out of the Habsburg monarchy, was culturally, ethnically and linguistically divided and FACED SEVERAL DIFFERENT LEGAL SYSTEMS WITH DIFFERENT CONSEQUENCES FOR WOMEN. MELISSA FEINBERG (ch. 3) analyses the Czech women's reform movement, JANA OSTERKAMP (ch. 4) examines the German and Slovak situation from a historical and legal perspective. Both scholars find COMMON DENOMINATORS OF THE FAILURE OF LEGAL REFORM BUT REACH DIFFERENT CONCLUSIONS — their chapters nevertheless complement each other in finding that WOMEN'S CLAIMS TO CHANGES IN FAMILY LAW MET WITH PERSISTENT RESISTANCE DESPITE THE ACTIVE ENGAGEMENT OF THE WOMEN'S RIGHTS MOVEMENT IN LEGAL QUESTIONS. And the key date: THE CONSTITUTIONAL PROVISIONS ON EQUALITY WERE NOT IMPLEMENTED UNTIL 1949, WHEN CZECHOSLOVAKIA UNDER COMMUNIST RULE ADOPTED A COMPREHENSIVE REFORM OF FAMILY LAW. This reflects a wider European pattern: FUNDAMENTAL CHANGES FOR WOMEN DID NOT ARRIVE TOGETHER WITH OTHER PROGRESSIVE REFORMS. In Poland, for instance, the women's rights movement REFUSED TO RECOGNISE THE VALIDITY OF HETERONOMOUS LEGAL CODES and could embark on legal battles only after achieving a degree of internal cohesion. (This chapter also covers MILADA HORÁKOVÁ, a member of the Women's National Council, who drafted changes to family law and worked for reforms across political lines.)

cards.q: When was constitutional equality implemented in Czechoslovak family law, and what does that show?
cards.a: ONLY IN 1949, UNDER COMMUNIST RULE, by a comprehensive reform of family law — although the constitutional provisions on equality had applied since 1918. It reflects a wider European pattern: FUNDAMENTAL CHANGES FOR WOMEN DID NOT ARRIVE TOGETHER WITH OTHER PROGRESSIVE REFORMS.
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

cards.q: Why did the Polish women's rights movement long refrain from legal battles?
cards.a: Because it REFUSED TO RECOGNISE THE VALIDITY OF HETERONOMOUS LEGAL CODES — law imposed from outside — and could embark on those battles only after achieving a degree of internal cohesion.
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

slides.title: Communism: rights on paper, mentalities unchanged
slides.text: The common features of European legal history DIVERGED WITH THE ADVENT OF COMMUNIST RULE. THE BOLSHEVIK FAMILY CODE OF 1918 formally ENDED THE SUBORDINATION OF WOMEN TO MEN IN THE FAMILY, LEGALISED DIVORCE and introduced PROTECTION FOR UNMARRIED MOTHERS, FOR WOMEN'S PAID WORK AND FOR THEIR PROPERTY. Its reform potential was in part undermined under STALIN'S LEADERSHIP (1924–1953), but equal rights for women were implemented in the laws of other eastern European countries under communist rule during and after the Second World War. The chapters by GORDANA STOJAKOVIĆ on Yugoslavia (ch. 7) and KRASSIMIRA DASKALOVA on Bulgaria (ch. 8) show the essential point: COMMUNISM CREATED CERTAIN OPPORTUNITIES FOR ADVANCING WOMEN'S RIGHTS, PARTICULARLY THROUGH EMPLOYMENT — BUT GENDER RELATIONS WITHIN THE FAMILY CHANGED VERY LITTLE IN THE FACE OF PERSISTENT MENTALITIES AND CULTURE.

cards.q: What did the Bolshevik family code of 1918 introduce?
cards.a: It formally ENDED THE SUBORDINATION OF WOMEN TO MEN IN THE FAMILY, LEGALISED DIVORCE and introduced protection for UNMARRIED MOTHERS, FOR WOMEN'S PAID WORK AND FOR THEIR PROPERTY. Its reform potential was in part undermined under Stalin's leadership (1924–1953).
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

cards.q: What is the conclusion about communism and women's rights (Yugoslavia, Bulgaria)?
cards.a: Communism created CERTAIN OPPORTUNITIES, particularly THROUGH EMPLOYMENT — BUT GENDER RELATIONS WITHIN THE FAMILY CHANGED VERY LITTLE IN THE FACE OF PERSISTENT MENTALITIES AND CULTURE.
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

slides.title: Scandinavia and the completion of reform in the 1960s and 1970s
slides.text: In the Scandinavian countries A DIFFERENT PATTERN applied. BY THE END OF THE 19TH CENTURY a first wave of legal reform had given UNMARRIED WOMEN THE RIGHT TO EDUCATION AND TO WORK, and married women gained some economic rights. IN DENMARK, FINLAND, ICELAND, NORWAY AND SWEDEN reforms of civil law and of private international law transformed women's position in marriage FROM THE END OF THE 19TH CENTURY INTO THE 1920s. Emancipation in family law was further eased by THE WEAKENING INFLUENCE OF RELIGION AND TRADITIONAL VALUES. The resulting EGALITARIAN NORDIC MODEL OF MARRIAGE became A SUCCESS TO BE IMITATED for women's organisations in other countries. ONLY IN THE 1960s AND 1970s did the western European countries achieve COMPREHENSIVE REFORM OF FAMILY LAW. Some of those reforms grew out of decades of effort in which the strategic arguments of 'CIVIC MATERNALISM' or 'SOCIAL HOUSEKEEPING' were used — that is, justifying reform on the ground THAT IT WOULD BENEFIT WOMEN'S MATERNAL ROLE AND STRENGTHEN THE FAMILY. Further reforms were then needed on EQUAL PAY FOR EQUAL WORK, TAX LAW, LEGISLATION ON PROSTITUTION and THE DIVISION OF LABOUR IN THE FAMILY.

terms.def: The strategic argument that reform will benefit women's maternal role and strengthen the family — not that woman is equal to man.

cards.q: What is 'civic maternalism' and why did the reformers stick to it?
cards.a: A strategic argument ('civic maternalism' / 'social housekeeping') that social and legal reform WILL BENEFIT WOMEN'S MATERNAL ROLE AND STRENGTHEN THE FAMILY. It was an argument not from equality but from usefulness — and it lay behind a large part of the reforms completed only in the 1960s and 1970s.
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

cards.q: How was the Scandinavian development different?
cards.a: Already by the end of the 19th century a first wave of reform gave UNMARRIED WOMEN the right to education and work and married women some economic rights; from the end of the 19th century into the 1920s reforms transformed their position in marriage. The WEAKENING INFLUENCE OF RELIGION helped, and an EGALITARIAN NORDIC MODEL OF MARRIAGE arose as a model to imitate.
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

slides.title: Why entry into the legal profession was a turning point
slides.text: IN EVERY EUROPEAN COUNTRY THE ENTRY OF WOMEN INTO LAW FACULTIES AND INTO THE PROFESSION WAS A WATERSHED EVENT THAT ILLUMINATED THE GENDERED CONSTRUCTION OF THE WHOLE FIELD — and their successes contributed to demolishing persistent cultural claims about the inferiority of the female intellect. The legal profession has its roots in the Enlightenment and IDEALISED RATIONALITY, OBJECTIVITY AND INTELLECTUAL RIGOUR, WHICH WERE TRADITIONALLY ASSOCIATED WITH MASCULINITY. In civil law and common law systems alike, legal education contributed to lawyers functioning as A COHESIVE SOCIAL GROUP — through privilege, a shared worldview and habitus. The requirements of legal education thus helped to create and maintain AN EXCLUSIVELY MALE ELITE in the profession and on the bench, which in turn influenced the judicial system, legislation and the academic understanding of law. Women's participation in the profession THREATENED AND ULTIMATELY CHANGED THAT PARADIGM. The resistance ran along two lines: ANTI-FEMINIST ARGUMENTS DENYING WOMEN THE CAPACITY FOR RATIONALITY AND OBJECTIVITY, and SEPARATELY THE ARGUMENT THAT WOMEN REPRESENTED A COMPETITIVE ECONOMIC THREAT TO AN ALREADY OVERCROWDED PROFESSION. Advocates of women's rights regularly objected that NO STATUTE OR REGULATION DENIED WOMEN ENTRY TO THE PROFESSION, and hence that their exclusion rested on A BIASED INTERPRETATION OF THE RULES. Some reformers also used THE RHETORIC OF MATERNALISM: affirming women's responsibility for the home while arguing for their extended role in the public sphere — women's moral purity and caring capacities could, it was said, CLEANSE CORRUPT POLITICS, STRENGTHEN THE NATION AND IMPROVE JUSTICE.

cards.q: Why was the legal profession so hard for women to penetrate?
cards.a: Because it IDEALISED RATIONALITY, OBJECTIVITY AND INTELLECTUAL RIGOUR, traditionally associated with MASCULINITY, and legal education made lawyers A COHESIVE SOCIAL GROUP with its own privilege and habitus — thereby maintaining AN EXCLUSIVELY MALE ELITE that shaped the courts, legislation and legal scholarship alike.
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

cards.q: What two lines of resistance did women face, and how were they answered?
cards.a: 1) The ANTI-FEMINIST argument that women are incapable of rationality and objectivity. 2) SEPARATELY, the economic argument that they were A COMPETITIVE THREAT to an already overcrowded profession. Against this it was objected that NO RULE DENIED WOMEN ENTRY and that their exclusion rested on A BIASED INTERPRETATION — and the rhetoric of maternalism was used as well.
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

slides.title: Lay advocates: a gap that was later closed
slides.text: The scholarly effort to find pioneers has revealed AN UNDERAPPRECIATED PATTERN: THE EMPLOYMENT OF WOMEN AS NON-PROFESSIONAL OR 'LAY' ADVOCATES. In the middle and second half of the 19th century women reached legal practice by various routes. In exceptional circumstances the Serbian widow MARIJA MILUTINOVIĆ-PUNKTATORKA (1810–1875) worked from 1847. In RUSSIA lay women advocates practised UNTIL ALEXANDER II FORBADE WOMEN TO ACT AS PRIVATE REPRESENTATIVES IN 1876. IN FINLAND (Korpiola, ch. 12) women worked as lay advocates IN THE 1880s AND 1890s. Similarly in SWEDEN, ANNA PETTERSSON SET UP HER OWN LAW OFFICE IN 1904, although she had not completed the traditional academic training or examinations. And the point: THAT EXCEPTIONAL ACCESS LASTED UNTIL THE GAPS IN THE LAW WERE CLOSED EITHER BY GOVERNMENTS OR BY CORPORATE PRESSURE FROM WITHIN THE PROFESSION ITSELF.

cards.q: What were 'lay advocates' and how did that route end?
cards.a: Women employed in legal practice as NON-PROFESSIONAL representatives without formal qualification — Marija Milutinović-Punktatorka in Serbia from 1847, lay advocates in Russia (until Alexander II's ban in 1876), in Finland in the 1880s and 1890s, Anna Pettersson in Sweden from 1904. THE GAP CLOSED as soon as GOVERNMENTS OR CORPORATE PRESSURE WITHIN THE PROFESSION closed it.
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

slides.title: Legal aid bureaux: where help turned into reform
slides.text: The German feminist LOUISE OTTO summed it up bitterly in 1890: 'WOMEN LEARN TO BEAR THE BURDEN OF THE LAW; THEY DO NOT STUDY IT.' To instruct women about their rights, many altruistic advocates founded LEGAL AID BUREAUX OR PROTECTIVE AGENCIES that helped women assert legal claims. And here is the mechanism worth remembering: THE DAILY PRACTICE OF THOSE AGENCIES SHARPENED FEMINISTS' AWARENESS OF THE ROLE OF LAW IN WOMEN'S LIVES — AND AT THE SAME TIME FORMED THE FIRST WOMEN LAWYERS, some of whom worked with disadvantaged groups. In ESTONIA, VERA POSKA-GRÜNTHAL (1898–1986) worked at the Bureau of Legal Advice, where her clients were women needing advice in family disputes and divorce; realising that THE BALTIC CIVIL CODE OF 1864 WAS OBSOLETE AND CONTRARY TO THE CONSTITUTION OF THE NEW ESTONIAN REPUBLIC, she joined the women's movement and, together with VILMA ANDERSON AND OLINDE ILUS, drafted a reform of family law. In the Czech lands MILADA HORÁKOVÁ of the Women's National Council drafted changes to family law and worked for reforms across political lines. Similarly women's legal knowledge intertwined with grassroots rights struggles in FRANCE, GERMANY AND ROMANIA. Despite national differences, those activists were united by A SHARED COMMITMENT TO SOCIAL JUSTICE WITHIN NETWORKS OF FEMALE SOLIDARITY.

cards.q: How did legal aid bureaux advance the women's movement?
cards.a: Their DAILY PRACTICE SHARPENED FEMINISTS' AWARENESS OF THE ROLE OF LAW IN WOMEN'S LIVES — and at the same time FORMED THE FIRST WOMEN LAWYERS. Example: Vera Poska-Grünthal at the Estonian Bureau of Legal Advice found that THE BALTIC CIVIL CODE (1864) WAS CONTRARY TO THE CONSTITUTION of the new republic, and with Vilma Anderson and Olinde Ilus drafted a reform of family law.
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

cards.q: How did Louise Otto sum up women's position towards the law in 1890?
cards.a: 'WOMEN LEARN TO BEAR THE BURDEN OF THE LAW; THEY DO NOT STUDY IT.'
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

slides.title: Studying law and the first women lawyers
slides.text: The rise of a feminist legal movement also depended on EDUCATIONAL AND PROFESSIONAL REFORMS. The expansion of primary and secondary education at the end of the 19th century markedly raised the number of women seeking university study. Admission to law faculties was GRADUAL AND PIECEMEAL: women could study law alongside men IN FRANCE AS EARLY AS THE 1880s, but in RUSSIA THEY WERE FORBIDDEN TO DO SO UNTIL 1916 AND IN HUNGARY UNTIL THE SECOND WORLD WAR. And an important mechanism: THE FACT THAT EDUCATIONAL AND EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITIES WERE NOT ALIGNED CAUSED PERSONAL HARDSHIP AND AT THE SAME TIME MOTIVATED WOMEN LAWYERS TO ADVOCACY WITHIN THE WOMEN'S RIGHTS MOVEMENT. The Swiss EMILIE KEMPIN-SPYRI (1853–1901) graduated from the University of Zurich IN 1887 and first worked in New York, where she taught law and, with American colleagues, provided legal services to the poor (1888–1891). The Belgian MARIE POPELIN (1846–1913), a 1888 graduate of the Free University of Brussels, fought unsuccessfully for the admission of women to the profession and lived her life as a teacher and political activist — SHE DID NOT LIVE TO SEE THE REFORM OF 1921 THAT ADMITTED WOMEN TO THE BELGIAN BAR. The Romanian SARMISA BILCESCU (1867–1935) studied law in Paris, returned to Bucharest and IN 1891 OBTAINED AUTHORISATION FROM THE BAR; even so ELLA NEGRUZZI (1876–1949) met resistance IN 1913 when seeking to register for the Romanian bar examination and was admitted ONLY IN 1920. In PRUSSIA women students were denied access TO THE EXAMINATIONS, which closed the law faculties to them. IN MOST COUNTRIES, HOWEVER, THE PATTERN OF EXCLUSION RESTRICTED ACCESS TO THE PROFESSION ITSELF — TO PUPILLAGE AND TO THE BAR ASSOCIATIONS — RATHER THAN TO UNIVERSITY STUDY.

cards.q: Where was the pattern of women's exclusion from law located — at study or at the profession?
cards.a: IN MOST COUNTRIES AT THE PROFESSION ITSELF — at PUPILLAGE AND THE BAR ASSOCIATIONS — rather than at university study. (The Prussian exception was the denial of access TO THE EXAMINATIONS, which closed the faculties to women.)
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

cards.q: Compare women's access to the study of law in France, Russia and Hungary.
cards.a: In FRANCE women could study law alongside men AS EARLY AS THE 1880s; in RUSSIA it was forbidden UNTIL 1916; in HUNGARY UNTIL THE SECOND WORLD WAR.
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

cards.q: What do the cases of Marie Popelin and Ella Negruzzi demonstrate?
cards.a: Popelin (1846–1913) graduated in Brussels in 1888, fought in vain for women's entry to the profession and DID NOT LIVE TO SEE THE REFORM OF 1921. Negruzzi met resistance in 1913 when registering for the Romanian bar examination and was admitted ONLY IN 1920 — although Sarmisa Bilcescu had obtained authorisation there as early as 1891. In short: ONE WOMAN'S BREAKTHROUGH DID NOT MEAN THE PROFESSION WAS OPEN.
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

slides.title: Admission to the bar: a map of dates
slides.text: THE OVERWHELMING MAJORITY OF EUROPEAN COUNTRIES ADMITTED WOMEN TO THE BAR BETWEEN THE TWO WORLD WARS: PORTUGAL (1918); SCOTLAND AND WALES (1920); NORTHERN IRELAND (1921); BELGIUM, CZECHOSLOVAKIA, ENGLAND AND GERMANY (1922); POLAND (1925); HUNGARY (1928); AUSTRIA (1929). In DENMARK women were admitted to the lower grades of the legal professions as early as 1906, but gained access to all positions ONLY IN 1919. In SWEDEN, FROM 1918 ONLY UNMARRIED WOMEN could practise. ITALY was one of the first countries where women fought for access, already in the 1880s, but they secured the right ONLY IN 1919. In HUNGARY women were forbidden to study law and the five or six women advocates practising after 1928 had studied abroad — AND IN 1937 A NEW STATUTE EXPRESSLY EXCLUDED THEM FROM THE BAR. In BULGARIA access came latest: VERA ZLATAREVA (1905–1977) was admitted as the first woman advocate IN 1944.

cards.q: When were women admitted to the bar in central Europe?
cards.a: The overwhelming majority of countries between the wars: Portugal 1918; Scotland and Wales 1920; Northern Ireland 1921; BELGIUM, CZECHOSLOVAKIA, ENGLAND AND GERMANY 1922; Poland 1925; Hungary 1928; Austria 1929.
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

cards.q: Which countries departed from that pattern?
cards.a: DENMARK admitted women to the lower grades as early as 1906, to all positions only 1919. SWEDEN from 1918 admitted ONLY UNMARRIED WOMEN. ITALY, where the fight began in the 1880s, only 1919. HUNGARY EXPRESSLY EXCLUDED women from the bar by a new statute in 1937. BULGARIA only 1944 (Vera Zlatareva).
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

slides.title: The bar is not the bench: a second, slower timeline
slides.text: One of the IMPORTANT DISCONTINUITIES in women's legal history is that ADMISSION TO THE BAR ASSOCIATIONS DID NOT NECESSARILY COINCIDE WITH ADMISSION TO THE JUDICIARY. In NORWAY the first woman judge at local level was admitted at HAMMERFEST IN 1913, but broader access for women to the judiciary came ONLY IN 1921. RUSSIA permitted women judges AFTER THE REVOLUTION OF 1917. In IRELAND FOUR WOMEN MAGISTRATES took office IN 1920. LITHUANIA had its first woman judge IN 1924, SWEDEN AND GERMANY IN 1927. In POLAND the first woman became a JUVENILE COURT JUDGE IN 1929. IN THE 1930s FINLAND AND CZECHOSLOVAKIA announced their first women judges, DENMARK followed IN 1933, and in the SPANISH republican zone of the civil war the first woman judge was appointed IN 1936. And then the contrast to remember: SOME COUNTRIES THAT GAVE WOMEN EARLY AND PIONEERING ACCESS TO THE PROFESSION NEVERTHELESS DENIED THEM THE BENCH UNTIL THE END OF THE SECOND WORLD WAR: ENGLAND 1945–1949, FRANCE 1946, AUSTRIA 1947. Others followed: THE NETHERLANDS (1947), BELGIUM (1948), GREECE (1959), ITALY (1963) and SWITZERLAND AND PORTUGAL ONLY IN 1974.

cards.q: Why must admission to the bar and to the bench not be confused?
cards.a: Because they DO NOT COINCIDE. England admitted women to the bar in 1922 but had its first women judges in 1945–1949; France judges in 1946, Austria in 1947 (bar 1929). Some countries with EARLY access to the profession denied the bench UNTIL THE END OF THE SECOND WORLD WAR.
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

cards.q: List the main dates of the first women judges.
cards.a: Norway: local level, Hammerfest 1913, broader access 1921. Russia 1917 (after the revolution). Ireland 1920 (four magistrates). Lithuania 1924. Sweden and Germany 1927. Poland 1929 (juvenile court judge). Finland and Czechoslovakia in the 1930s, Denmark 1933, Spain 1936. After the war: the Netherlands 1947, Belgium 1948, Greece 1959, Italy 1963, Switzerland and Portugal 1974.
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

slides.title: Why women lawyers mattered more than the numbers
slides.text: The chapters on Poland, Bulgaria, France, Spain, Germany, Belgium and Yugoslavia document A SIGNIFICANT CONNECTION BETWEEN THE PROFESSIONAL AND THE POLITICAL EMANCIPATION OF WOMEN. And here is why it is more than a statistic: HAVING WOMEN INSIDE THE LEGAL PROFESSIONS WAS A NEW STEP IN THE HISTORY OF WOMEN'S RIGHTS, BECAUSE ONCE WOMEN BECAME LEGAL EXPERTS THEY COULD CHALLENGE THE SYSTEM FROM WITHIN THE PROFESSION — AND THEY DID SO. In some states even from within the government system. ANNE LOGAN'S study (ch. 11) of women in the development of CRIMINOLOGY shows how women's early experience in charity and social work expanded into criminal law advocacy in England: feminists active in prison reform called for legal changes improving the treatment of prisoners, and THEIR INTERNATIONAL NETWORKING AND RESEARCH CONTRIBUTED TO THE CREATION OF CRIMINOLOGY AND TO THEIR OWN REINVENTION AS 'CRIMINOLOGISTS'.

cards.q: Why was women's entry into the profession a qualitatively new step?
cards.a: Because ONCE WOMEN BECAME LEGAL EXPERTS THEY COULD CHALLENGE THE SYSTEM FROM WITHIN THE PROFESSION — and in some states from within the government system too. Until then they could only criticise the law from outside.
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

cards.q: How, on Anne Logan's account, are women connected with the birth of criminology?
cards.a: Women's early experience in CHARITY AND SOCIAL WORK expanded into criminal law advocacy; feminists active in PRISON REFORM called for better treatment of prisoners, and THEIR INTERNATIONAL NETWORKING AND RESEARCH CONTRIBUTED TO THE CREATION OF CRIMINOLOGY — and to their own reinvention as 'CRIMINOLOGISTS'.
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

slides.title: FIFCJ 1928: the first international legal sorority
slides.text: Among the reform societies of the interwar period was THE FIRST TRANSNATIONAL ASSOCIATION OF WOMEN LAWYERS AND JUDGES: THE INTERNATIONAL FEDERATION OF WOMEN IN LEGAL AND JURIDICAL CAREERS (FIFCJ). It sought to create bonds of 'FRIENDSHIP AND SOLIDARITY', to facilitate women's access to 'all juridical careers', to 'improve the professional conditions of women', to study the laws and to 'SPREAD THE IDEA OF WORLD PEACE'. It was founded IN 1928 by an alliance of women lawyers and judges from ESTONIA, GERMANY, FRANCE, SPAIN, POLAND AND BRITAIN and appears to have been THE FIRST VIABLE AND MOST INFLUENTIAL INTERNATIONAL LEGAL SORORITY of its day (after the short-lived American 'Woman's International Bar Association' of 1888). Officially the FIFCJ was neutral and 'apolitical', BUT AS EARLY AS 1929 IT WAS RECOGNISED AS A NON-GOVERNMENTAL ORGANISATION WITH THE RIGHT TO ADDRESS THE LEAGUE OF NATIONS. Conferences were held in PARIS (1929, 1930, 1937), NAPLES (1934) AND VIENNA (1936); BY 1936 members claimed to represent THIRTY-SEVEN COUNTRIES. As participants in 'internationalism', the FIFCJ women used LEGAL PRECEDENTS, LEGAL ARGUMENTS AND THE LEGAL SITUATION OF WOMEN IN OTHER EUROPEAN STATES AS COMPARATIVE SUPPORT for arguments in favour of reform — thereby making women's questions a matter of international importance. The end is dark: THE INFILTRATION OF FASCIST MEMBERS, PARTICULARLY FROM ITALY AND GERMANY, TOGETHER WITH ACTIVE DISCRIMINATION AGAINST WOMEN, SHATTERED ANY APPEARANCE OF UNITY BY 1936 — and the consequences for women lawyers under the German Reich or in the occupied countries were DEVASTATING.

terms.def: The International Federation of Women in Legal and Juridical Careers (1928) — the first transnational association of women lawyers and judges.

cards.q: What was the FIFCJ, when was it founded and how did it end?
cards.a: THE FIRST TRANSNATIONAL ASSOCIATION OF WOMEN LAWYERS AND JUDGES, founded IN 1928 by women from Estonia, Germany, France, Spain, Poland and Britain; recognised in 1929 as a NON-GOVERNMENTAL ORGANISATION with the right to address the League of Nations, and by 1936 claiming to represent 37 countries. THE INFILTRATION OF FASCIST MEMBERS FROM ITALY AND GERMANY shattered any appearance of unity by 1936.
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

cards.q: What method of argument did the FIFCJ use?
cards.a: A COMPARATIVE one: it used LEGAL PRECEDENTS, LEGAL ARGUMENTS AND THE LEGAL SITUATION OF WOMEN IN OTHER EUROPEAN STATES as support for reform at home — thereby making women's questions a matter of INTERNATIONAL IMPORTANCE.
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

slides.title: The ICW and the national councils: the infrastructure of reform
slides.text: Legal reform was a CORNERSTONE of the programmes of women's rights organisations in the BELLE ÉPOQUE. IN 1878 the FIRST INTERNATIONAL CONGRESS ON WOMEN'S RIGHTS IN PARIS discussed the legal oppression of women and the arguments for reform. THE INTERNATIONAL COUNCIL OF WOMEN (ICW, FOUNDED IN 1888 IN THE UNITED STATES) and its national branches gave priority to reforming women's position in law, with consequences for Europe too. IN 1900 in Paris, at the SECOND INTERNATIONAL CONGRESS OF WOMEN'S WORKS AND INSTITUTIONS, legally educated women — the Belgian MARIE POPELIN, the French JEANNE CHAUVIN and the German ANITA AUGSPURG — debated legal questions with the leadership, including the ICW president MAY WRIGHT SEWALL. The ICW inspired the creation of national associations which then coordinated their efforts and sent delegates to its international meetings: the German BUND DEUTSCHER FRAUENVEREINE (BDF) was founded IN 1894 precisely in response to the ICW's call; the French CONSEIL NATIONAL DES FEMMES FRANÇAISES (CNFF) IN 1901 for women's legal and social questions — THE EQUALITY OF SPOUSES IN FAMILY LAW, EQUAL EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITIES, EQUAL PAY FOR EQUAL WORK, POLITICAL RIGHTS AND AN INDEPENDENT NATIONALITY FOR MARRIED WOMEN. BY 1903 TEN NATIONAL COUNCILS had formed. According to ANNE COVY'S research (ch. 13), the legislative committee of the Portuguese CNMP, founded in Lisbon IN 1914, devoted A THIRD OF ITS EFFORTS to juridical questions. The ICW also staffed specialised committees — to its committee on law it appointed the French advocate MARIA VÉRONE (1874–1938), who after the First World War defended women's rights AT THE LEAGUE OF NATIONS.

cards.q: How did the ICW function as the infrastructure of reform?
cards.a: The International Council of Women (ICW, 1888, USA) INSPIRED THE CREATION OF NATIONAL ASSOCIATIONS which then coordinated efforts and sent delegates to its meetings — the German BDF (1894), the French CNFF (1901), ten national councils by 1903. The ICW also staffed specialised committees (appointing the advocate Maria Vérone to its committee on law).
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

cards.q: What programme did the French CNFF (1901) set itself?
cards.a: THE EQUALITY OF SPOUSES IN FAMILY LAW, EQUAL EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITIES, EQUAL PAY FOR EQUAL WORK, POLITICAL RIGHTS FOR WOMEN and AN INDEPENDENT NATIONALITY FOR MARRIED WOMEN.
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

slides.title: Citizenship, the nationality of married women, and Geneva
slides.text: Among the most important transnational legal questions were CITIZENSHIP AND THE RIGHT OF MARRIED WOMEN TO THEIR OWN NATIONALITY. REGINA WECKER (ch. 14) uses the history of Swiss citizenship to show how THE GENDERING OF CITIZENSHIP made the search for equality exceptionally difficult where the process is complicated by several further factors including MUNICIPAL BELONGING AND LOCAL LEGAL CUSTOMS — adding that globalisation further complicates the search for individual rights, so that 'the battle for equality continues'. CATHERINE JACQUES (ch. 15) documents the UNEQUAL STRUGGLE of feminist activists who, though versed in law and politics, found it hard to make headway in DIPLOMATIC CIRCLES on questions of international law. In the interwar years those activists gave priority to REFORM OF THE LAW ON THE NATIONALITY OF MARRIED WOMEN AND OF FAMILY LAW in seeking access to the LEAGUE OF NATIONS. Their associations regarded international law as a 'NEUTRAL VEHICLE FOR SOLVING THE WORLD'S MOST COMPLEX QUESTIONS' and understood law as A MORAL AND RATIONAL FORCE — WHICH IS AN ECHO OF THE GROTIAN TRADITION of international law. As activists in non-governmental organisations, WOMEN LAWYERS THUS PLAYED A PART IN THE REBIRTH OF 'INTERNATIONAL SOCIETY'. SUSAN ZIMMERMANN (ch. 16) adds a further central theme of women's transnational engagement in Geneva: THE REGULATION OF LABOUR AS INFLUENCED BY RACE AND GENDER. Both chapters underline that women's engagement in the LEAGUE OF NATIONS AND THE INTERNATIONAL LABOUR ORGANIZATION (ILO) demonstrates both their skill in legal argument and their investment in those organisations as a means of securing women's rights.

cards.q: Which two questions were the main transnational legal themes of interwar feminism?
cards.a: CITIZENSHIP and THE RIGHT OF MARRIED WOMEN TO THEIR OWN NATIONALITY, together with family law — the activists gave them priority in seeking access to the LEAGUE OF NATIONS. Susan Zimmermann adds THE REGULATION OF LABOUR as influenced by race and gender at the ILO.
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

cards.q: How did women's associations understand international law, and why is that Grotian?
cards.a: As a 'NEUTRAL VEHICLE FOR SOLVING THE WORLD'S MOST COMPLEX QUESTIONS' and as A MORAL AND RATIONAL FORCE — which is AN ECHO OF THE GROTIAN TRADITION. As activists in non-governmental organisations, women lawyers thus played a part in THE REBIRTH OF 'INTERNATIONAL SOCIETY'.
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

slides.title: Conclusion: comparing laws as a weapon
slides.text: In the struggle for equal rights the leading figures of the European women's movement — and especially the women lawyers associated with it — advanced LEGAL REFORM AS THE SOLUTION TO THE TENSION BETWEEN RESTRICTIVE SOCIAL NORMS AND WOMEN'S DESIRE FOR EQUALITY. And this is the methodological point of the whole book, worth having ready: WITHIN THE WOMEN'S RIGHTS MOVEMENT, THE COMPARISON OF LAWS AND LEGAL SYSTEMS CONSTITUTED AN ESSENTIAL BODY OF KNOWLEDGE USED IN NATIONAL CONTEXTS TO PRESSURE GOVERNMENTS. Women's rights associations were nationally rooted, but many activists saw their struggles AT THE SAME TIME AS PART OF A LARGER EUROPEAN — IF NOT GLOBAL — CONTEST FOR LIBERTY, EQUALITY AND SORORITY. The authors close by turning to the present: questions of gender in the intersecting spheres of FAMILY LAW, LABOUR LAW, POLITICAL RIGHTS AND CITIZENSHIP continue to resonate in an interconnected world — and IN THE LIGHT OF THE CURRENT PROJECT OF A COMMON EUROPEAN CIVIL CODE THEY HOPE THAT EUROPEAN LEGISLATORS WILL LEARN FROM THE PAST.

cards.q: What role did the comparison of laws play in the women's rights movement?
cards.a: It was AN ESSENTIAL BODY OF KNOWLEDGE USED IN NATIONAL CONTEXTS TO PRESSURE GOVERNMENTS: the associations were nationally rooted, but the activists saw their struggles at the same time as part of a larger EUROPEAN — if not global — contest for liberty, equality and sorority.
cards.topic: HERstory — the legal position of women through the centuries

cards.q: What practical appeal does the book end with?
cards.a: In the light of THE CURRENT PROJECT OF A COMMON EUROPEAN CIVIL CODE the authors hope that EUROPEAN LEGISLATORS WILL LEARN FROM THE PAST — that is, that they will not repeat what the 19th-century codifications did.
